# Mechanical Engineering: the major (designed, parked)

*Designed 2026-10-08; not scheduled. Course data: `curriculum.json` (generated by `scripts/build_stem_majors.py`); the picture:
`DAG.md`. Shape follows `notes/major-design.md`. Course syllabi get written when a course is about to start.*

## TL;DR
- **What it is:** an ABET-shaped mechanical engineering major: the math/physics/chemistry base, the engineering sciences
  (statics, dynamics, mechanics of materials, thermodynamics, fluids, heat transfer, materials, circuits, control), then the
  mechanical core (mechanisms, vibrations, machine design, manufacturing, energy systems). Level II is the graduate core.
- **Written for a high-school graduate** (start: MA100 Precalculus).
- **Your entry point:** **Statics (ES211), Thermodynamics (ES221), Materials (ES240) and Engineering graphics/CAD (ES150).**
  Your computer engineering degree had the math, PHYS 211/212, CHEM 110, circuits (EE 210) and probability, but no engineering
  mechanics, so Statics is where the new material starts.
- **Size from your entry point:** ≈ 306 lessons of Level I core (≈ 5.9 years half-time, ≈ 2.9 years full-time).
  **If you do Unified Engineering first**, ME adds only five courses (mechanisms, vibrations, machine design, energy systems, PDEs:
  ≈ 94 lessons), because the engineering sciences are the same courses in both.
- **Books:** the engineering-science books are mostly in the library (Hibbeler, Cengel, Cengel & Cimbala, Callister). The
  mechanical core needs Norton, Rao, Shigley and Kalpakjian. Statics uses a free open textbook.

## 1. Plan
**Why (draft; correct it in MISSION.md):** a "good for the soul" major for understanding how machines and physical things work,
with hands-on outlets that already exist in your life: woodworking (your library has a whole shelf), 3D printing, and the
3D chess set as a physical object.

**Shape.** Most ABET-accredited mechanical programs share this outline: the math and science base, the engineering sciences,
the design and manufacturing courses, and a capstone. Courses that every engineering discipline takes have **ES** numbers and
are shared, one course each, with the Unified Engineering major. **ME** numbers are the mechanical-only courses.

**Book choices (judgment, with the library's limits).**
- *Statics:* Hibbeler is in the library only as a grade C copy (chapters only, nothing quoted), so the primary is Baker & Haynes,
  *Engineering Statics: Open and Interactive*, a free CC-licensed book with interactive diagrams [2]. Your Hibbeler copy supplies
  extra problems by exercise number.
- *Mechanics of materials:* Hibbeler again, also grade C. It needs reconversion before lessons can quote it; Philpot is the
  fallback to acquire.
- *Thermodynamics and heat transfer:* Cengel's combined *Introduction to Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer* (in the library) for
  ES221 and ES370, with Cengel & Boles to acquire for the energy-systems course.
- *Control:* Åström & Murray, *Feedback Systems*; its book site is fbsbook.org [3].
- *Practice:* the FE Mechanical practice-problem book (grade A, in the library) is a ready-made self-check after the
  engineering sciences (ME390). Taking the actual FE exam is optional and only matters if you'd want a PE license.

**Where you enter (Penn State BS Computer Engineering, 2026 bulletin [1]).** Credited: MATH 140/141/220/231/250 (and the math
degree), PHYS 211/212, CHEM 110, EE 210 (circuits and devices), STAT 418 or 414 (probability), CMPSC 121/122 (programming).
"Maybe": ES160 (numerical methods: you can program, but numerical methods for engineers may be new) and MA412 (PDEs).
EE 353 (signals and systems) covers the Laplace-transform half of ES340 Control, so that course will move faster.

## 3. How it would run (when it starts)
- One lesson = two 25-minute blocks: reading with a guide, then a lesson page built around worked problems (free-body diagram →
  equations → numbers → sanity check), with several varied problems per idea.
- Every lesson ends with **Extra practice (optional)**: book problems with changed numbers, an FE-style problem where one fits,
  and one article (a failure analysis, a how-it's-made piece, a classic design story).
- **Units** are checked by code, not by eye: answers go through the math widget with expressions allowed, and every worked number
  is computed (with a units library where it matters) before it's shown.
- **Making things** is the optional practice: ME385 (shop work with your woodworking books), ES150 (CAD with OpenSCAD and
  FreeCAD), and the capstone (a mechanism you design and build).
